newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland Unionists, Sinn Fein plan TV debate.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland Unionists, Sinn Fein plan TV debate.

text.p: Northern Ireland's key adversaries, Protestant unionists and the Catholic-backed Sinn Fein, will hold a rare television debate next Tuesday in advance of multi-party peace talks.
The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), said they would take part in a discussion to be transmitted by the British Broadcasting Corporation.
It will bring together two ideologically opposed parties who have been sharply critical of each other for much of the past three decades and who have yet to sit at the same negotiating table.

The UUP, Northern Ireland's key Protestant party committed to continued British rule, will be represented by Ken Maginnis, its security spokesman and a fierce critic of the IRA's guerrilla war to unite the province with Ireland.
Sinn Fein will be represented by its chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, who will lead the party at the peace talks if it is allowed to join them in September.
The two men in recent years have traded barbs over the airwaves but never in the same studio.

The UUP decided last month to take part in television debates with Sinn Fein because UUP officials feared that they were losing a propaganda war against their long-time foes by refusing direct talks with them.

Sinn Fein wants the peace talks to start dismantling British rule of Northern Ireland. Britain says this can only happen if a majority of people in the province, currently 60 percent pro-British, want it.
The UUP wants the province to remain part of the United Kingdom and says Britain is being tricked by the Irish government and Sinn Fein into considering surrendering sovereignty over it.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said on Wednesday that Sinn Fein would be allowed to take part in the peace talks providing the IRA's July 20 ceasefire is deemed genuine and credible.

Maginnis is on record as saying that the IRA ceasefire, its second since 1994, is a ruse aimed at getting Sinn Fein to the peace talks and will break down if Sinn Fein does not get its way at the negotiations.

He believes that the IRA will not end its guerrilla campaign against British troops, Northern Ireland police and strategic targets until Sinn Fein gets its way and the province becomes part of Ireland.

McGuinness has repeatedly denied being a senior member of the IRA. He says Sinn Fein wants a permanent peace in Northern Ireland which could only be brought about when the province is merged with the Irish republic.
The two parties are supposed to take part in peace talks starting September 9 but it is not yet known whether the UUP will sit at the same table with Sinn Fein.
The UUP wants guarantees that the IRA will start disarming to prove that its war is over for good and show it will not resume hostilities if a final settlement is not to its liking.
McGuinness says the IRA has said in the past that it will not surrender a single bullet until a final settlement is agreed and told reporters on Wednesday that he knew of no change to that policy.
